490	\section{Quantum registers and EPR states}
   491	% Paper label sec:lin-reg kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   492	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   493	
   494	\begin{definition}[State space of a linear register]\label{def:lin-reg}
   495		\uses{def:complementary}
   496		For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension
   497		$|V|$, endowed with the canonical orthonormal basis
   498		$\{\ket{x}\}_{x \in V}$. A \emph{quantum state on $V$} is a unit vector
   499		$\ket{\psi}_V \in \C^V$. If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_i$ is a direct sum of
   500		subspaces over $\F$, then $\C^V$ is identified with
   501		$\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{V_i}$ by identifying
   502		$\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus x_k}$ with
   503		$\ket{x_1} \ot \dots \ot \ket{x_k}$. In particular, a basis $\{e_i\}$ of
   504		$V$ yields the decomposition $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k (\F e_i)$ and hence
   505		$\C^V = \bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{|\F|}$; the factors $\C^{|\F|}$ are called
   506		the \emph{qudits} of $\C^V$.
   507	\end{definition}
   508	
   509	\begin{definition}[EPR state]\label{def:EPR}
   510		\uses{def:lin-reg}
   511		For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, the \emph{EPR state} on
   512		$\C^V \ot \C^V$ is
   513		\[
   514			\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_V
   515			= \frac{1}{\sqrt{|V|}} \sum_{x \in V} \ket{x} \ot \ket{x}\;.
   516		\]
   517		We write $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_{\F_q}$ and
   518		$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$.
   519	\end{definition}
   520	
   521	\section{Generalized Pauli observables}
   522	% Paper label sec:generalized-pauli kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   523	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
   524	
   525	\begin{definition}[Generalized Pauli observables]\label{def:generalized-pauli}
   526		\uses{def:subfield-trace, def:lin-reg}
   527		Let $p$ be a prime and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$. The \emph{generalized Pauli
   528		observables over $\F_p$} are the unitaries on $\C^{\F_p}$ given by
   529		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-fp}
   530			\sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   531			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   532			\sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \omega^{bj} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   533		\end{equation}
   534		for $a, b \in \F_p$, with arithmetic over $\F_p$. For $q = p^k$, the
   535		\emph{generalized Pauli observables over $\F_q$} are the unitaries on
   536		$\C^{\F_q}$
   537		\[
   538			\tau^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   539			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   540			\tau^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \omega^{\tr(bj)} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   541		\]
   542		for $a, b \in \F_q$, where $\tr$ here denotes $\tr_{q \to p}$
   543		(Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}); for admissible $q$ this agrees with
   544		the standing shorthand, $p = 2$, and $\omega = -1$, so that all phases are
   545		signs. All the $\tau^X$ operators commute with one another, as do all the
   546		$\tau^Z$ operators. Their common eigenbases consist of the vectors
   547		$\ket{e_W}$, labeled by $e \in \F_q$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
   548		\[
   549			\ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{j \in \F_q}
   550			\omega^{-\tr(ej)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
   551			\ket{e_Z} = \ket{e}\;;
   552		\]
   553		the Fourier transform
   554		\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-f}
   555			F = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b \in \F_q}
   556			\omega^{-\tr(ab)} \ket{a}\bra{b}
   557		\end{equation}
   558		maps the computational ($Z$) eigenbasis to the $X$ eigenbasis. We write
   559		$\{\tau^W_e\}_{e \in \F_q}$ for the projective measurement whose elements
   560		are the rank-one projectors onto the vectors of the $W$ eigenbasis. For
   561		systems of $n$ qudits, we write, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a \in \F_q^n$,
   562		\[
   563			\tau^W(a) = \tau^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \tau^W(a_n)\;, \qquad
   564			\ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}
   565		\]
   566		for $e \in \F_q^n$, with associated rank-one projectors $\tau^W_e$.
   567	\end{definition}
   568	
   569	\begin{lemma}[Product and twisted commutation relations]\label{lem:twisted-commutation}
   570		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   571		Let $q = p^k$, let $n \ge 1$ be an integer, and let $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   572		\begin{enumerate}
   573			\item For all $a, a' \in \F_q$ and $b \in \F_p$,
   574			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
   575				      \tau^W(a)\, \tau^W(a') = \tau^W(a + a')
   576				      \qquad \text{and} \qquad
   577				      \bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^b = \tau^W(ab)\;;
   578			      \end{equation}
   579			      in particular $\bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^p = \Id$, so each
   580			      $\tau^W(a)$ is a unitary with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots
   581			      of unity.
   582			\item For all $a, b \in \F_q^n$,
   583			      % Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   584			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fq}
   585				      \tau^X(a)\, \tau^Z(b)
   586				      = \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^Z(b)\, \tau^X(a)\;,
   587			      \end{equation}
   588			      where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i \in \F_q$. The case
   589			      $q = p$, $n = 1$ reads
   590			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fp}
   591				      \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b)
   592				      = \omega^{-ab}\, \sigma^Z(b)\, \sigma^X(a)
   593				      \qquad \text{for all } a, b \in \F_p\;.
   594			      \end{equation}
   595		\end{enumerate}
   596	\end{lemma}
   597	\begin{proof}
   598		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   599		All identities are verified on computational basis states. For the product
   600		relations with $W = X$, shifting twice by $a'$ and $a$ equals shifting by
   601		$a + a'$; with $W = Z$, the phases $\omega^{\tr(aj)}\omega^{\tr(a'j)}$
   602		combine by $\F_q$-linearity of the trace, and the power relation follows by
   603		iterating. For the scalar twisted commutation,
   604		$\tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$, while
   605		$\tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(b(j+a))}\ket{j + a} =
   606		\omega^{\tr(ab)}\,\omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$. The multi-qudit relation
   607		follows by applying the scalar relation factor by factor and summing the
   608		exponents, using $\tr(a \cdot b) = \sum_i \tr(a_i b_i)$. For $q = p$ the
   609		trace is the identity map, which gives \eqref{eq:twisted-fp}.
   610	\end{proof}
   611	
   612	\begin{lemma}[Fourier cancellation over a subspace]\label{lem:cancellation}
   613		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal, def:subfield-trace}
   614		Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_q^k$ and let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$, where
   615		$p$ is the characteristic of $\F_q$ and $\tr = \tr_{q \to p}$. For all
   616		$v \notin V^\perp$,
   617		\[
   618			\E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr(\bu \cdot v)} = 0\;,
   619		\]
   620		where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $\bu$ in $V$.
   621	\end{lemma}
   622	\begin{proof}
   623		This is Fact 3.2 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Since $v \notin V^\perp$,
   624		the $\F_q$-linear functional $u \mapsto u \cdot v$ is not identically zero
   625		on $V$, hence surjective onto $\F_q$; composing with the nonzero map $\tr$
   626		shows that there is $u_0 \in V$ with $\tr(u_0 \cdot v) \neq 0$. Writing $C$
   627		for the expectation, translation invariance of the uniform distribution on
   628		$V$ gives
   629		$C = \E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr((\bu + u_0) \cdot v)}
   630		= \omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)}\, C$, and $\omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)} \neq 1$
   631		forces $C = 0$.
   632	\end{proof}
   633	
   634	\begin{lemma}[Fourier expansion of Pauli observables]\label{lem:pauli-observable-expansion}
   635		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   636		For every integer $n \ge 1$, all $W \in \{X, Z\}$, and all $a \in \F_q^n$,
   637		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   638		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj}
   639			\tau^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \F_q^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^W_b\;,
   640		\end{equation}
   641		and conversely
   642		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
   643			\E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\, \omega^{-\tr(\ba \cdot b)}\, \tau^W(\ba)
   644			= \sum_{b' \in \F_q^n} \E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\,
   645			\omega^{\tr(\ba \cdot (b' - b))}\, \tau^W_{b'}
   646			= \tau^W_b\;.
   647		\end{equation}
   648	\end{lemma}
   649	\begin{proof}
   650		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, lem:cancellation}
   651		Each $\ket{b_W}$ is an eigenvector of $\tau^W(a)$ with eigenvalue
   652		$\omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}$: for $W = Z$ this is immediate from the
   653		definition, and for $W = X$ it follows from the single-qudit computation
   654		$\tau^X(a)\ket{e_X} = \omega^{\tr(ae)}\ket{e_X}$, applied factor by factor.
   655		Expanding $\tau^W(a)$ in the orthonormal eigenbasis
   656		$\{\ket{b_W}\}_{b \in \F_q^n}$ gives the first display. For the inversion,
   657		substitute the first display and exchange the order of summation; by
   658		Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation} applied with $V = \F_q^n$ (so that
   659		$V^\perp = \{0\}$), the inner expectation vanishes unless $b' = b$, where
   660		it equals $1$.
   661	\end{proof}
   662	
   663	Since only admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ arise in the Pauli basis test, the
   664	maximally entangled state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ and the qudit Pauli
   665	projectors are isomorphic to tensor products of qubit EPR states
   666	$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$ and qubit Pauli projectors. This is the content of the
   667	next lemma, which is what allows the Pauli basis test to self-test Pauli
   668	observables and maximally entangled states over \emph{qubits}
   669	(Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}).
   670	
   671	\begin{lemma}[Qudit-to-qubit isomorphism]\label{lem:pauli-binary}
   672		\uses{def:admissible-size, def:binary-representation,
   673			def:generalized-pauli, def:EPR}
   674		For all admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ and integers $L$, there exists an
   675		isomorphism $\phi : (\C^q)^{\ot L} \to (\C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ such that
   676		\begin{equation}\label{eq:epr-q-to-epr-2}
   677			\phi \ot \phi\, \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot L}
   678			= \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot Lk}
   679		\end{equation}
   680		(applying the natural identifications between
   681		$(\C^q)^{\ot L} \ot (\C^q)^{\ot L}$ and $(\C^q \ot \C^q)^{\ot L}$, and
   682		between $(\C^2)^{\ot Lk} \ot (\C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ and
   683		$(\C^2 \ot \C^2)^{\ot Lk}$). Moreover, for all $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and all
   684		$u \in \F_q^L$,
   685		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-q-to-pauli-2}
   686			\tau^W_u = \phi^\dagger\,
   687			\Bigl(\bigotimes_{i=1}^L \bigotimes_{j=1}^k
   688			\sigma^W_{u_{ij}}\Bigr)\, \phi\;.
   689		\end{equation}
   690		Here $(u_{ij})_{i,j}$ is the array of $\F_2$ values with
   691		$u_i = \sum_j u_{ij} e_j$ for all $i \in \{1, \dots, L\}$, where
   692		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ is the fixed self-dual normal basis of $\F_q$ over
   693		$\F_2$ of Definition~\ref{def:binary-representation}; and for
   694		$i \in \{1, \dots, L\}$ and $j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$ the $(i,j)$-th factor
   695		$\sigma^W_{u_{ij}}$ denotes the projector
   696		$\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\Id + (-1)^{u_{ij}} \sigma^W(1)\bigr)$ acting on the
   697		$s$-th qubit, where $s = (i-1)k + j$.
   698	\end{lemma}
   699	\begin{proof}
   700		\uses{lem:pauli-observable-expansion, lem:downsize_field,
   701			lem:twisted-commutation}
   702		Define the isometry $\theta : \C^q \to (\C^2)^{\ot k}$ by
   703		$\theta\ket{a} = \ket{a_1} \ot \dots \ot \ket{a_k}$, where
   704		$\kappa(a) = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ is the binary representation with respect
   705		to the fixed basis; since $\kappa$ is a bijection, $\theta$ is a unitary
   706		and $\theta \ot \theta\, \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_{2^k}} =
   707		\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot k}$. For $a \in \F_q$ with
   708		$\kappa(a) = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$, the inversion formula of
   709		Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-observable-expansion} gives
   710		$\tau^W_a = \E_{b \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(ab)}\, \tau^W(b)$; writing
   711		$b = \sum_j b_j e_j$, self-duality of the basis gives
   712		$b_j = \tr(b e_j)$ (item 1 of Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field}) and hence
   713		$\tr(ab) = \sum_j a_j b_j$. The product relation of
   714		Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation} factors
   715		$\tau^W(b) = \prod_j \tau^W(b_j e_j)$, so the expectation factors over
   716		independent $b_1, \dots, b_k \in \F_2$. A computation on basis states shows
   717		that for all $c \in \F_2$, $\tau^W(c e_j) = \theta^\dagger\,
   718		\sigma^{W,j}(c)\, \theta$, where $\sigma^{W,j}(c)$ is the identity for
   719		$c = 0$ and the Pauli $W$ observable acting on the $j$-th qubit of
   720		$(\C^2)^{\ot k}$ for $c = 1$. Averaging,
   721		$\E_{b_j \in \F_2} (-1)^{a_j b_j} \sigma^W(b_j) =
   722		\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\Id + (-1)^{a_j}\sigma^W(1)\bigr) = \sigma^W_{a_j}$,
   723		whence $\tau^W_a = \theta^\dagger \bigl(\bigotimes_j
   724		\sigma^W_{a_j}\bigr) \theta$. Taking $\phi = \theta^{\ot L}$ and tensoring
   725		the last identity over the $L$ qudits, using
   726		$\tau^W_u = \bigotimes_{i=1}^L \tau^W_{u_i}$, yields both displayed
   727		identities.
   728	\end{proof}
   729	
   730	\begin{remark}\label{rem:pauli-binary-source}
   731		In the source statement of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-binary} in
   732		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, the index range of the qubit factor is printed as
   733		$j \in \{1, \dots, q\}$; the intended range, used above, is
   734		$j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$, as the $i$-th qudit is mapped to $k$ qubits.
   735	\end{remark}

171	\section{Finite fields, traces, and self-dual bases}
   172	% Paper labels sec:finite-fields, sec:subfields, sec:ff-representations kept
   173	% for cross-reference fidelity.
   174	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   175	\label{sec:subfields}
   176	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   177	
   178	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   179	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   181	
   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a subfield of
   184		$\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$ over $\F_q$.
   185		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   186		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   187		\[
   188			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   189			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   190		\]
   191		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   192		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   193		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   194		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   195		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   196		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   197		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   198		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   199		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   200		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   201		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   202		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   203		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   204		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   205	\end{definition}
   206	
   207	\begin{definition}[Admissible field size]\label{def:admissible-size}
   208		A field size $q$ is \emph{admissible} if $q = 2^k$ for an odd integer $k$.
   209	\end{definition}
   210	
   211	Only fields $\F_{2^k}$ with $k$ odd are used in the analysis of the Pauli basis
   212	test.
   213	
   214	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   215		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   216		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   217		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   218		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   219			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   220		\end{equation}
   221		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   222		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   223		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   224		be seen from the equivalent formula
   225		\[
   226			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   227		\]
   228		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   229	\end{definition}
   230	
   231	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   232		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   233		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   234		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   235		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   236		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   237		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   238		$\{\alpha^{q^j}\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$, that
   239		basis is called a \emph{normal basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not
   240		exist for every field extension, but for $q = 2$ and odd $k$ a self-dual
   241		normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ always exists; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}
   242		exhibits one through an explicit construction.
   243	\end{definition}
   244	
   245	\begin{lemma}[Coordinate maps of self-dual bases]\label{lem:downsize_field}
   246		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace,
   247			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   248		Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer, and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis of
   249		$\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The map $\kappa_q$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$
   250		satisfies:
   251		\begin{enumerate}
   252			\item for all $x \in \F_{q^k}$,
   253			      $\kappa_q(x) = \bigl(\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_1), \dots,
   254			      \tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_k)\bigr)$;
   255			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   256			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
   257			\item for all $M \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in \F_{q^k}^n$,
   258			      $\chi_q(M)\, \kappa_q(v) = \kappa_q(Mv)$.
   259		\end{enumerate}
   260		Items 1 and 2 use self-duality; item 3 holds for an arbitrary basis.
   261	\end{lemma}
   262	\begin{proof}
   263		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   264		For item 1, write $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$, multiply both sides by $e_j$, and
   265		take traces: $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j)
   266		= x_j$ by self-duality. For item 2, expand
   267		$xy = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j e_i e_j$ and take traces; self-duality retains
   268		exactly the diagonal terms, giving $\sum_i x_i y_i = \kappa_q(x) \cdot
   269		\kappa_q(y)$. For item 3, the $i$-th block of $\kappa_q(Mv)$ equals
   270		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   271		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.
   272	\end{proof}
   273	
   274	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   275		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   276		Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ a self-dual normal basis of
   277		$\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$. Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and the
   278		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones
   279		vector in $\F_2^k$.
   280	\end{lemma}
   281	\begin{proof}
   282		\uses{lem:downsize_field}
   283		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   284		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   285		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   286		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$
   287		would vanish identically on $\F_{2^k}$ by linearity; but then item 1 of
   288		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} would give $\kappa(b) =
   289		(\tr(b e_1), \dots, \tr(b e_k)) = 0$ for every $b$, contradicting the
   290		bijectivity of $\kappa$. Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and item 1 of
   291		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   292		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.
   293	\end{proof}
   294	
   295	\begin{definition}[Binary representation of field elements]\label{def:binary-representation}
   296		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size,
   297			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   298		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and
   299		for all, a self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   300		$\F_2$ together with its multiplication tables
   301		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});
   302		the maps $\kappa$ and $\tr$ always refer to this basis. The \emph{binary
   303		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   304		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   305		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   306		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   307		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   308			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)
   309			= \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \bigl(K_{e_i}\, \kappa(b)\bigr)\;,
   310		\end{equation}
   311		where $\kappa(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$.
   312	\end{definition}

429	\section{Lines}
   430	
   431	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   432	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   433	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   434	
   435	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   436		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   437		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   438		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   439			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   440		\end{equation}
   441		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   442		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   443		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   444		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   445		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   446		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   447		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   448		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   449	\end{definition}
   450	
   451	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   452		\uses{def:line}
   453		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   454		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   455	\end{proposition}
   456	\begin{proof}
   457		\uses{def:line}
   458		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   459		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   460		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   461		inclusion.
   462	\end{proof}
   463	
   464	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   465	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   466	representation is obtained as follows.
   467	
   468	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   469		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   470		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   471		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   472		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   473		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   474		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   475		\[
   476			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   477		\]
   478		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   479		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   480		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   481		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   482		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   483		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   484		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   485		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   486		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   487		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   488	\end{definition}

   926	\subsection{Linear spaces and registers}
   927	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   928	
   929	For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension $|V|$.
   930	The space $\C^V$ is endowed with a canonical orthonormal basis
   931	$\{\ket{x}\}_{x\in V}$.
   932	By ``a quantum state on $V$'' we mean a unit vector
   933	\begin{equation*}
   934	  \ket{\psi}_V \in \complex^V\;.
   935	\end{equation*}
   936	If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_k$ is the direct sum of subspaces $V_k$ over $\F$,
   937	then $\complex^V$ can be identified with $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k
   938	\complex^{V_i}$, by the identification of $\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus
   939	  x_k}$ with $\ket{x_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \ket{x_k}$.
   940	As a special case, if $\{e_i\}$ is a basis of $V$ the decomposition $V =
   941	\bigoplus_{i=1}^k ( \F e_i)$ yields the tensor product decomposition $\C^V =
   942	\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{\abs{\F}}$.
   943	We sometimes refer to the spaces $\C^{\abs{\F}}$ as the ``qudits'' of $\C^V$ (or
   944	of a state on it).
   945	
   946	\begin{definition}
   947	  \label{def:EPR}
   948	  For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, define the \EPR state on $\C^V
   949	  \otimes \C^V$ by
   950	  \begin{equation*}
   951	    \ket{\EPR}_V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\abs{V}}} \sum_{x\in V}\ket {x}\otimes \ket{x}\;.
   952	  \end{equation*}
   953	  We also write $\ket{\EPR}_{\F_q}$ as $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}$ as
   954	  $\ket{\EPR}$.
   955	\end{definition}
   956	
   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}
  1004	
  1005	We will make frequent use of Naimark dilation. In our setting, it can be formulated as follows. For a proof, see~\cite[Theorem 5.1]{ML20}
  1006	
  1007	\begin{theorem}[Naimark dilation]\label{thm:naimark}
  1008	Let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in $\mH_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \mH_{\mathrm{B}}$.
  1009	Let $A = \{A^x_a\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\mH_{\mathrm{A}}$
  1010	and $B=\{B^y_b\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\mH_{\mathrm{B}}$.

   121	  $[\alpha]_k$ halts within $T$ steps on input $x$ then $\cal{U}_k$ halts in at most $C(k \cdot |\alpha| \cdot |x| \cdot T)^c$ steps and the contents

   126	Thus, the Turing machine $\cal{A}$ can simulate $\cal{B}$ on input $(x,x^2)$ as follows: it first computes

   144	\paragraph{Hardwiring constants.} 
   145	Throughout this paper, we often define Turing machines $\cal{M}$
   146	with some number $k$ of inputs, and then for some string $a \in \{0,1\}^*$
   147	define a $(k-1)$-input Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ whose behavior on input
   148	$(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$ is to execute $\cal{M}$ on input
   149	$(a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   150	Informally, the Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ ``hardwires'' the input $a$ onto the
   151	first tape of $\cal{M}$.
   152	We  informally write $\cal{M}_a(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1}) =
   153	\cal{M}(a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   154	
   155	More precisely, the Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ on input $(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$ first
   156	computes the encoding $e = \mathrm{enc}_{k+1}(\desc{\cal{M}},a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$, and then runs the
   157	universal Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$ on input $e$.
   158	The description of $\cal{M}_a$ can be computed from $\desc{\cal{M}}$ and $a$ in
   159	time $O(|a| + |\cal{M}| + O(1))$, where the $O(1)$ comes from the description
   160	length of the universal Turing machine $\cal{U}_k$.
   161	
   162	Furthermore, the time complexity of the Turing machine $\cal{M}_a$ on input
   163	$(y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$ is at most \\ $\poly(|a|,|y_1|,\ldots,|y_{k-1}|,T)$ where $T$
   164	is the time complexity of $\cal{M}$ on input $(a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   165	This bound comes from the complexity of encoding the inputs from the $k$ tapes
   166	into the $\mathrm{enc}_{k+1}(\cdot)$ format, and then simulating $\cal{M}$ on input
   167	$(\desc{\cal{M}},a,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1})$.
   168	
   169	
   170	
   171	\paragraph{Description complexity bounds.} When we bound the description lengths of
   172	the Turing machines presented in this paper, we do not worry about the exact
   173	details of how Turing machines are represented as binary strings -- as mentioned we assume that
   174	\emph{some} reasonable encoding is used -- but instead
   175	we distinguish between whether the Turing machine 
   176	description depends on any parameters used elsewhere in the paper. Note that whether the \emph{description} depends on any parameters is different from whether the Turing machine takes parameters as \emph{input}. For example, consider the following (high-level) descriptions of Turing machines $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$:
   177	
   178	\begin{enumerate}
   179		\item Turing machine $\cal{A}$ takes two inputs $(\alpha,x)$ and outputs the integer $\alpha \times x$ where $\alpha, x$ are interpreted as positive integers written in binary. 
   180		\item Turing machine $\cal{B}$ takes one input $x$ and outputs the integer $\beta \times x$ where $\beta$ is a fixed positive integer.
   181	\end{enumerate}
   182	
   183	The description of $\cal{A}$ does not depend on any ``external'' parameters, so its description length $|\desc{\cal{A}}|$ is some universal constant, which we express as $O(1)$. On the other hand, the description of $\cal{B}$ depends on some fixed integer $\beta$; in other words, the parameter $\beta$ is ``hard-wired'' into $\cal{B}$'s description. The description of $\cal{B}$ can be taken to be the following: $\cal{B}$ (which is a $1$-input Turing machine) simulates the execution of the $2$-input Turing machine $\cal{A}$ where the first input tape of $\cal{A}$ has the binary representation of $\beta$ written onto it and the second input tape has $x$ (which is provided as input to $B$) written into it. Thus the description of $\cal{B}$ includes the binary representation of $\beta$, the description of $\cal{A}$ (whose length is a universal constant), and the description of the universal Turing machine (whose length is a universal constant). Thus the description length of $\cal{B}$ is $O(\log \beta) + O(1) = O(\log \beta)$.
   184	
   185	
   186	
   187	\paragraph{Time complexity bounds.} When we bound the time complexity of the Turing machines presented in this paper, we similarly do not worry about the exact
   188	implementation details, but instead we assume that basic computations such as integer arithmetic, string comparisons, etc.\ are all performed
   189	using reasonably efficient algorithms that run in polynomial time in the length of the input. When running other Turing machines as subroutines, we assume that there is some polynomial overhead due to \Cref{thm:universal-tm}.
   190	
   191	
   192	\paragraph{Timeout counters.} We sometimes define Turing machines that are required to halt if 
   193	either the Turing machine or some subroutine takes a number of time steps that exceeds some specified threshold. For example, we may write ``Let $\cal{M}$ be the Turing machine that on input the description $\ol{\cal{R}}$ of a Turing machine $\cal{R}$ and an integer $T$, simulates $\cal{R}$ on the empty tape and halts if more than $T$ steps are performed.''
   194	
   195	This is useful for establishing an \emph{a priori} bound on the time complexity of the Turing machine. In particular we will be able to claim that $\cal{M}$, as described above, always runs in time at most $\poly(T,|\ol{\cal{R}}|$, irrespective of the running time of $\cal{R}$ itself.
   196	
   197	We explain how such a Turing machine can be realized formally. We use a variant of the universal Turing machine of \Cref{thm:universal-tm}. Using the theorem, it is straightforward to show that given a (single tape) Turing machine $\cal{R}$ there exists another two-tape Turing machine $\cal{M}'$ such that, whenever the second tape is initialized to the binary representation of $T$, $\cal{M}'$ simulates $\cal{R}$ and in-between every simulated step of $\cal{R}$, decrements the second tape and checks if it reaches zero. If it does, then $\cal{M}'$ halts and rejects. Otherwise, it continues. 
   198	
   199	The time complexity of $\cal{M}'$ is, by definition, at most $O(T \log T)$ for all inputs. The description length of $\cal{M}'$ is at most $O(|\ol{\cal{R}}|)$, because this is the description size of the universal Turing machine, whose initial tape has been hardwired with $\ol{\cal{R}}$.
   200	To convert back to a single tape Turing machine and obtain $\cal{M}$ from $\cal{M}$' we can use \Cref{thm:universal-tm} again, at the cost of a polynomial blow-up in the time complexity.
   201	
   202	
   203	\paragraph{Input representations.} 
   204	Although the inputs and outputs of a Turing machine are strictly speaking
   205	  binary strings, we oftentimes slightly abuse notation and specify Turing
   206	  machines that treat their inputs and outputs as objects with more structure,
   207	  such as finite field elements, integers, symbols from a larger alphabet, and
   208	  so on.
   209	  In this case we implicitly assume that the Turing machine specification uses a
   210	  consistent convention to represent these structured objects as binary strings.
   211	  Conventions for objects such as integers are straightforward.
   212	  For representations of finite field elements, we refer the reader to
   213	  Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.

   216	\subsection{Linear spaces}
   217	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
   218	
   219	Linear spaces considered in the paper generally take the form $V = \F^n$ for a
   220	finite field $\F$ and integer $n \geq 1$.
   221	In particular, when we write ``let $V$ be a linear space'', unless explicitly
   222	stated otherwise we always mean a space of the form $\F^n$.
   223	Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \ldots, \hat{e}_n\}$ denote the standard basis of $V$, where for
   224	$i \in\{ 1, 2, \ldots, n\}$,
   225	\begin{equation*}
   226	  \hat{e}_i = (0, \ldots, 0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)
   227	\end{equation*}
   228	has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere.
   229	We write $\End(V)$ to denote the set of linear transformations from $V$ to
   230	itself.
   231	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]
   232	  A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
   233	  subset of the standard basis of $V$.\footnote{The use of the term ``register''
   234	    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often
   235	    partitioned into ``registers'' containing a few qubits each.}
   236	  We often represent such a subspace as an indicator vector $u\in \{0,1\}^s$,
   237	  where $s=\dim(V)$, such that if $\{\hat{e}_1,\ldots,\hat{e}_s\}$ is the standard basis of
   238	  $V$ then $S = \text{span}\{\hat{e}_i|\,u_i=1\}$.
   239	\end{definition}
   240	
   241	\begin{definition}
   242	  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
   243	  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
   244	  define the \emph{dot product}
   245	  \begin{equation*}
   246	    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
   249	  \begin{equation*}
   250	    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
   251	    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
   252	  \end{equation*}
   253	  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
   254	  space will always be clear from context.
   255	\end{definition}
   256	
   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
   261	However, the following remains true over all fields.
   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}
   270	\end{lemma}
   271	
   272	\begin{proof}
   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
   282	\end{proof}
   283	
   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}
   321	
   322	
   323	\begin{remark}
   324	We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
   325	a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
   326	independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}
   331	
   332	\begin{remark}
   333	  Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V$.
   334	  Suppose subspace $S$ is a register subspace of $V$ spanned by
   335	  $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$.
   336	  Then it is not hard to verify that the canonical complement of $\hat{E}_{0}$ is
   337	  $\hat{E}\setminus \hat{E}_0$ and the span of the canonical complement coincides with
   338	  $S^\perp$.
   339	\end{remark}
   340	
   341	
   342	\begin{lemma}
   343	  \label{lem:canonical-complement}
   344	  Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors $F = \{v_1,\ldots,v_m \}
   345	  \subseteq V$ and let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$ as defined
   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   347	  Let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   348	  Then
   349	  \begin{equation*}
   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}
   352	\end{lemma}
   353	
   354	\begin{proof}
   355	To show the first item, we must show that every vector in $V$ can be
   356	written as a sum of an element of $S$ and an element of $T$. To do
   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose
   358	rows are the vectors $v_i$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   359	  Write $A = U B$ where $U$ is invertible and $B$ is in reduced row echelon
   360	  form.
   430	For general background on finite fields, and explicit algorithms for elementary
   431	arithmetic operations, we refer to~\cite{mullen2013handbook}.
   432	
   433	\subsubsection{Subfields and bases}
   434	\label{sec:subfields}
   435	Let $q$ be a prime power and $k$ an integer. 
   436	The field $\Fq$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of
   437	dimension $k$ over $\Fq$.
   438	Let $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ be a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ as a linear space over $\Fq$.
   439	Introduce a bijection $\downsize_q : \F_{q^k} \rightarrow \Fq^k$ between
   440	$\F_{q^k}$ and $\Fq^k$ defined with respect to the basis $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ by
   441	\begin{equation*}
   442	  \downsize_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k
   443	\end{equation*}
   444	where $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$.
   445	This map satisfies several nice properties.
   446	First, the map is an isomorphism of $\Fq$-vector spaces: it is $\Fq$-linear and addition in $\F_{q^k}$
   447	naturally corresponds to vector addition in $\Fq^k$.
   448	Namely, for all $a,b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   449	\begin{equation*}
   450		\downsize_q (a + b) = \downsize_q(a) + \downsize_q(b)\;.
   451	\end{equation*}
   452	Second, multiplication by a field element in $\F_{q^k}$ corresponds to a linear
   453	map on $\F_{q}^k$.
   454	For all $a \in \F_{q^k}$, there exists a matrix $K_a \in \Matrix_k (\Fq)$ such
   455	that for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   456	\begin{equation*}
   457		\downsize_q (a b) = K_a \, \downsize_q(b)\;.
   458	\end{equation*}
   459	The matrix $K_a$ is called the \emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to
   460	  basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$}.
   461	
   462	We extend the map $\downsize_q$ to vectors, matrices and sets over $\F_{q^k}$.
   463	For $v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$, define
   464	\begin{equation*}
   465	  \downsize_q (v) = \bigl( \downsize_q (v_i) \bigr)_{i=1}^n \in \Fq^{kn}\;.
   466	\end{equation*}
   467	Similarly, for matrix $M = (M_{i, j}) \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$, define
   468	\begin{equation*}
   469	  \downsizem_q (M) = \bigl( K_{M_{i, j}} \bigr) \in \Matrix_{mk, nk} (\Fq)\;,
   470	\end{equation*}
   471	the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th block is the multiplication table $K_{M_{i,
   472	    j}}$ of $M_{i, j}$ with respect to basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$.
   473	For a set $S$ of vectors in $\F_{q^k}^n$, define
   474	\begin{equation*}
   475		\downsize_q(S) = \{ \downsize_q(v) : v \in S \}\;.
   476	\end{equation*}
   477	We omit the subscript and write $\downsize$ and $\downsizem$ for $\downsize_q$
   478	and $\downsizem_q$ respectively when $q$ equals to $p$, the characteristic of
   479	the field.
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}
   521	\end{lemma}
   522	 
   523	\begin{proof}
   524	  We show each property by direct calculation.
   525	  \begin{enumerate}
   526	    \item Let $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Then by the definition of
   527	    $\downsize_q$, $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$. Multiplying both sides by $e_j$
   528	    and taking the trace yields $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i
   529	    \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j) = x_j$, where the last equality is by
   530	    self-duality of the basis.
   531	    \item Write $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ and $\downsize_q(y) =
   532	      (y_1, \dots, y_k)$. Then
   533	      \begin{align*}
   534	        \tr_{q^k \to q} (xy) &= \tr_{q^k \to q}(\sum_{ij} x_i y_j e_i
   535	                               e_j) \\
   536	                             &= \sum_{ij} x_i y_j \tr_{q^k \to q}(  e_i
   537	                               e_j) \\
   538	                             &= \downsize_q(x) \cdot \downsize_q(y),
   539	      \end{align*}
   540	      where the last equality uses the self-duality of the basis.
   541	    \item
   542	      We compute the $i$th $\F_q^k$-block of $\downsize_q(Mv)$:
   543	      \begin{align*}
   544	        \downsize_q(Mv)_i &= \sum_{ij} \downsize_q(M_{ij} v_j) \\
   545	                          &= \sum_{ij} K_{M_{ij}} \downsize_q(v_j) \\
   546	                          &= \downsizem_q(M)_{ij} \downsize_q(v_j) ,
   547	      \end{align*}
   548	      where we have applied the definition of the multiplication table
   549	      $K_{M_{ij}}$ and the map $\downsizem_q(\cdot)$.
   550	  \end{enumerate}
   551	\end{proof}
   552	
   553	For $z\in \F^n$ and $V,W$ a pair of complementary subspaces, recall from
   554	Definition~\ref{def:complementary} the notation $z^V$ for the projection of $z$
   555	onto $V$ and parallel to $W$.
   556	
   557	\begin{lemma}
   558	  \label{lem:downsize_subspace}
   559	  Let $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ denote the map corresponding to a
   560	  basis $\{e_i\}$ for $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   561	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_{q^k}^n$ with linearly independent basis
   562	  $\{b_1,\ldots,b_t\} \subseteq \F_{q^k}^n$.
   563	  Then the following hold:
   564	  \begin{enumerate}
   565	 	\item $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace of $\,\F_{q}^{nk}$.
   566		\item $\{ \downsize_q(e_i b_j) \}_{i,j}$ is a linearly independent basis of
   567	    $\downsize_q(V)$ over $\F_q$.
   568		\item Let $V, W$ be complementary subspaces of $\F_{q^k}^n$.
   569	    Then $V' = \downsize_q(V)$ and $W' = \downsize_q(W)$ are complementary
   570	    subspaces of $\F_q^{kn}$, and furthermore for all vectors $z \in
   571	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsize_q(z^V) = \downsize_q(z)^{V'}$ and
   572	    $\downsize_q(z^W) = \downsize_q(z)^{W'}$.
   573	  \end{enumerate}
   574	\end{lemma}
   575	
   576	\begin{proof}
   577	  For the first item, we first verify that $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace.
   578	  Since $V$ is a subspace, it contains $0 \in \F_{q^k}^n$, and therefore $\downsize_q(0)
   579	  = 0$ is also in $\downsize_q(V)$.
   580	  Let $u', v' \in \downsize_q(V)$.
   581	  Using that $\downsize_q$ is a bijection there exist $u,v \in \F_{q^k}^n$ such that
   582	  $u' = \downsize_q(u)$ and $v' = \downsize_q(v)$. Therefore
   583	  \[
   584	    u' + v' = \downsize_q(u) + \downsize_q(v) =
   585	    \downsize_q(u + v) \in \downsize_q(V)\;,
   586	  \]
   587	  where the inclusion follows because $V$ is a subspace and thus contains $u +
   588	  v$.
   589	  Finally, for all $x' \in \F_{q}$, for all $v \in V$, we have that $x'
   590	  \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(x' v)\in \downsize_q(V)$ where we used that $V$
   591	  is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q^k}$ and thus by $\F_q$ (since
   592	  $\F_q$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$).
   593	  Thus $\downsize_q(V)$ is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q}$.
   594	
   595	  For the second item, note that an element $v \in V$ can be expressed uniquely
   596	  as $v = \sum_{i = 1}^t v_i b_i$ for $v_i \in \F_{q^k}$.
   597	  The element $v_i$ can further be written as $\sum_j v_{i, j} e_j$ where $v_{i,
   598	    j} \in \F_q$.
   599	  Thus $v$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ e_j b_i \}$, and therefore
   600	  $\downsize_q(v)$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ \downsize_q (e_j
   601	  b_i) \}$.

references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:6:Our results establish the existence of transformations on \emph{families} of nonlocal games $\{\game_n\}_{n\in \N}$ having certain properties. In order to keep track of efficiency (and ultimately, computability) properties it is important to have a way to specify such families in a {uniform} manner. Towards this we introduce the following formalism. A \emph{uniformly generated family of games} is specified through a pair of Turing machines $\verifier = (\sampler,\decider)$ that satisfy certain conditions, in which case the pair is called a \emph{normal form verifier}. The Turing machine $\sampler$ (called a \emph{sampler}) takes as input an index $n \in \N$ and returns the description of a procedure that can be used to sample questions $(x,y)$ in the game (this procedure itself obeys a certain format associated with ``conditionally linear'' distributions, defined below). The Turing machine $\decider$ (called a \emph{decider}) takes as input an index $n$, questions $(x,y)$, and answers $(a,b)$, and returns a single-bit decision. For the sake of this proof overview we assume that the sampling and decision procedures run in time polynomial in the index $n$; we refer to the running time of these procedures as the \emph{complexity} of the verifier. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:71:	To overcome these difficulties we identify a natural class of question distributions, called \emph{conditionally linear distributions}, that generalize the low-degree test distribution. We show that conditionally linear distributions can be ``introspected'' using conditionally linear distributions only, enabling recursive introspection. (In particular, they are a rich enough class to capture the types of question distributions produced by the compression scheme of~\cite{NW19}.) We define normal form verifiers by restricting their sampling procedure to generate conditionally linear question distributions, and this allows us to obtain the compression procedure on normal form verifiers described in Theorem~\ref{thm:compression-informal}. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:73:	Conceptually,  the identification of a natural class of distributions that is ``closed under introspection'' is a key step that enables the introspection technique to be applied recursively. (As we will see later, other closure properties of conditionally linear distributions, such as taking direct products, play an important role as well.) Since conditionally linear distributions are central to our construction we describe them next. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:78:Fix a vector space $V$ that is identified with $\F^m$, for a finite field $\F$ and integer $m$. Informally (see Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} for a precise definition), a function $L$ on $V$ is \emph{conditionally linear} (CL for short) if it can be evaluated by a procedure that takes the following form: (i) read a substring $z^{(1)}$ of $z$; (ii) evaluate a linear function $L_1$ on $z^{(1)}$; (iii) repeat steps (i) and (ii) with the remaining coordinates $z\backslash z^{(1)}$, such that the next steps are allowed to depend in an arbitrary way on $L_1(z^{(1)})$ but not directly on $z^{(1)}$ itself. What distinguishes a function of this form from an arbitrary function is that we restrict the number of iterations of (i)---(ii) to a constant number (at most $9$, in our case). (One may also think of CL functions as ``adaptively linear'' functions, where the number of ``levels'' of adaptivity is the number of iterations of (i)---(ii).) A distribution $\mu$ over pairs $(x,y) \in V\times V$ is called {conditionally linear}  if it is the image under a pair of {conditionally linear functions} $L^\alice,L^\bob: V\to V$ of the uniform distribution on $V$, i.e.\ $(x,y)\sim (L^\alice(z),L^\bob(z))$ for uniformly random $z\in V$. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:80:An important class of CL distributions are low-degree test distributions, which are distributions over question pairs $(x,y)$ where $y$ is a randomly chosen affine subspace of $\F^m$ and $x$ is a uniformly random point on $y$. We explain this for the case where the random subspace $y$ is one-dimensional (i.e.\ a line). Let $V = V_\xpt \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ where $V_\xpt = V_{\dir{}} = \F^m$. Let $L^\alice$ be the projection onto $V_\xpt$ (i.e. it maps $(x,v) \to (x,0)$ where $x \in V_\xpt$ and $v \in V_{\dir{}}$). Define $L^\bob: V \to V$ as the map $(x,v) \mapsto (L^\lnf_v(x),v)$ where $L^\lnf_v: V_\xpt \to V_\xpt$ is a linear map that, for every $v \in V_{\dir{}}$, projects onto a complementary subspace to the one-dimensional subspace of $V_\xpt$ spanned by $v$ (one can think of this as an ``orthogonal subspace'' to the span of $\{ v \}$). $L^\bob$ is conditionally linear because it can be seen as first reading the substring $v \in V_{\dir{}}$ (which can be interpreted as specifying the \emph{direction} of a line), and then applying a linear map $L^\lnf_v$ to $x \in V_\xpt$ (which can be interpreted as specifying a canonical point on the line $\ell = \{ x + tv : t \in \F \}$). It is not hard to see (and shown formally in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game}) that the distribution of $(L^\alice(z),L^\bob(z))$ for $z$ uniform in $V$, is identical (up to relabeling) to the low-degree test distribution $(x,\ell)$ where $\ell$ is a uniformly random affine line in $\F^m$, and $x$ is a uniformly random point on $\ell$.
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:90:We say a few words about the design of $\mu'$ and the associated introspection game, which borrow heavily from~\cite{NW19}. Building on the ``quantum low-degree test'' introduced in~\cite{natarajan2018low} it is already known how a verifier can force a pair of players to measure $m$ EPR pairs in either the computational or Hadamard basis and report the (necessarily identical) outcome $z$ obtained, all the while using questions of length polylogarithmic in $m$ only. The added difficulty is to ensure that a player obtains, and returns, precisely the information about $z$ that is contained in $L^\alice(z)$ (resp. $L^\bob(z)$), and not more. A simple example is the line-point distribution described earlier: there, the idea to ensure that e.g.\ the ``point'' player only obtains the first component, $x$ of $(x,v) \in V_\xpt \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the verifier demands that the ``point'' player measures their qubits associated with the space $V_{\dir{}}$ in the Hadamard, instead of computational, basis; due to the uncertainty principle this has the effect of ``erasing'' the outcome in the computational basis.  The case of the ``line'' player is a little more complex: the goal is to ensure that, conditioned on the specification of the line $\ell$ received by the ``line'' player, the point $x$ received by the ``point'' player is uniformly random within $\ell$. This was shown to be possible in~\cite{NW19}.

## Review

Changes are required. Several defects are inherited from the QPBT paper, but the blueprint currently presents them as valid definitions, lemmas, or proofs. Those cases need a policy-compliant local correction and paper-gap verdict rather than silently copying the defect.

F1. The construction in `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-320`, label `def:canonical-complement`, takes pivot columns from reduced row echelon form. Since RREF is unique for a row space, two bases of the same subspace give the same complement. Remove the basis-dependence claims here and at lines 141-142; dependence is only on the subspace and fixed ambient standard basis.

F2. In `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:94-103`, label `lem:symmetric-strat`, the argument starts with a strategy for every `ε' > ε`. Neither it nor lines 110-122 produce a finite-dimensional strategy attaining `val*`, which line 74 defines as a supremum. State the approximate conclusion or supply an actual attainment theorem.

F3. Primary label `lem:ld-sandwich` at `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:465-495` contains the same transposition, but the cited `references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex:952-973`, label `fact:low-degree-sandwich`, uses `G^k_{g_k}⋯G^1_{g_1}⋯G^k_{g_k}`. The current `G^k_{g_1}` is undefined when the outcome types differ; `k = 0` is also undefined. Apply the documented local correction and handle the empty case.

F4. Source label `def:graph-distribution` at `references/qpbt-paper/07_types.tex:65-82` has the same boundary omission. With no edges, `m = k = 0`, so `1/(2m-k)` is undefined and the displayed mass is not a probability distribution. Require a nonempty edge set.

F5. The paper explicitly permits zero directions at `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:106-116` and samples them at lines 230-237, while its predicate at lines 380-384 asks for “the” `t` satisfying `x=u₀+tv'`. When `v'=0`, every `t` works and a dishonest nonconstant answer gives different values. Specify a canonical zero-direction branch or change and rejustify the distribution.

F6. `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:442-457` prints the same erroneous Reed–Solomon claim. Degree-at-most-`d` evaluation on all `q` points has parameters `[q,d+1,q-d]` when `d<q`, not `[q,d+1,q-d+1]`; for `d≥q`, even the dimension claim fails. Correct the provider argument and split the parameter regimes.

F7. Source `def:admissible` at `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-960` requires both an admissible binary field size and `m | q`. Line 235 instead quantifies arbitrary naturals and assumes only divisibility, allowing values for which `F_q` or `tr_{q→2}` is unavailable. Scope the distribution, predicate, and completeness result to an admissible tuple.

F8. Source `def:graph-distribution` assigns equal mass `1/(2m-k)` to every ordered supported pair. Sampling an undirected edge uniformly and then orienting it assigns loops mass `1/m` and oriented nonloops mass `1/(2m)`, which differs whenever loops occur; this graph has a loop at every vertex. Sample uniformly from ordered support.

F9. Source label `lem:delta-bound` at `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1520-1558` makes the same unsupported comparison. For allowed `a=1`, `b=1/2`, hence `c=4`, and `R=5`, the definitions give `k=9` and `m=8`. Bound `2^{-bm}` directly using `m ≥ (c/2) log R`; the lemma appears salvageable without `k≤m`.

F10. Source `fact:omega-anticomm-prob` at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:70-92` is inconsistent with the encoding defined at `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:873-897`. For admissible `(q,m,d)=(2,1,0)`, the actual anticommuting probability is `1/8`, while the second displayed lower bound is `1/2`. Require `d≥1` throughout and replace the false assertion that `ind_m(u)` vanishes exactly at zero.

F11. The source at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:95-109` concludes only `A≈_δB`; the blueprint adds the exact sentence `‖(A-B)ψ‖²≤δ`. On a singleton distribution, `A=√(2δ)I`, `B=0` satisfies an `O(δ)` premise but violates that exact bound. Retain `O(δ)` or strengthen the hypothesis explicitly.

F12. The public `lem:qld-win-implications` is unrestricted, but its proof establishes the conditional estimates only under `6md≤q` and then appeals to the later `thm:pauli`; the source has the same gap at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:244-258`. Moreover, `δ_qld≥1` does not trivialize the unsquared norm bound in `thm:pauli`. Prove the unconditional constant mass directly, for example from `ind_m(u)·ind_m(v)=∏ᵢ(1+uᵢ+vᵢ)` in characteristic two.

F13. `def:ld-game` requires its dimension to divide `q`, but lines 898-906 instantiate it with `2m+2`; admissibility only gives `m | q`. For power-of-two `m≥2`, `2m+2=2(m+1)` has an odd factor and cannot divide power-of-two `q`. The same unsupported application occurs at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1278-1284`; a soundness theorem with a compatible sampler is required.

F14. Source `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:917-924` defines `Dec` by replacing non-Boolean cube values with zero. For `q=8`, `m=d=1`, and constant `g=c∉{0,1}`, `Dec(g)=0` while `g(u)=c`. Lines 98-113 and 170-176 use this false identity, so the defect propagates through `lem:qld-construct-the-paulis`, `eq:qld-unitary-6`, `lem:qld-unitary`, and `thm:pauli`.

F15. From `lem:twisted-commutation`, the exact phase is `(-1)^{tr(e_j e_{j'}(u·v))}` for every pair `j,j'`. Self-duality does not make this vanish after multiplication by arbitrary `u·v`. For odd extension degree at least three, take `u=e_j^{-1}` and `v=e_{j'}^{-1}` in one coordinate: the phase is `(-1)^{tr(1)}=-1` even when `j≠j'`. The source claim at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1451-1456` is therefore also false.

F16. Source label `lem:qld-unitary` at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1765-1783` has the same gap. Without a small-`δ_S` condition, `1-2δ_S-√δ_S` can be negative and the EPR projection can be zero, making `aux₀/‖aux₀‖` undefined. Add a small-error case split and use an arbitrary auxiliary state with a trivial large-error bound in the other branch.

F17. Existing `blueprint/src/chapter/ch03_preliminaries.tex:74-78` and `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/Polynomials.lean:25-29` keep polynomial representatives rather than quotienting by evaluation. The new reduced-exponent function presentation identifies, for example, `0` and `X^q-X` when `d≥q`. Preserve the established representation or introduce a separately named evaluation-function object with the necessary restriction.

F18. Property 2 of `lem:qld-sublines` gives each projected point’s marginal separately, while `eq:qld-xz-lines-restricted` assumes a joint product distribution of both line-point pairs. The stronger joint law may follow from the construction, but it is not stated or proved. The source makes the same unsupported inference at `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1241-1245`; remove this redundant route or prove the joint law.

F19. The PR record contains only template comments. Populate the required sections with the QPBT source ranges, the declarations introduced, known paper discrepancies, and the actual validation commands.

No Lean source or blueprint `\lean`/`\leanok` links changed, and the changed chapters contain no direct `sorry`, `admit`, `axiom`, or proof-integrity bypass. I did not rerun the build under the read-only review contract; the PR record reports successful local CI. Residual risk remains in externally imported Ji–Natarajan–Vidick–Wright–Yuen and Coladangelo–Stark results, which were checked only as represented by the in-repository source mirrors.

   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:15:The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds.    980	        2m+2}(\F_q)$ defined by

   537			$i, j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, and, conditioned on
   538			$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, the point $u_X$ is uniformly random on $\ell_X$

   553		$v = (v_X, v_Z, \alpha_0, \beta_0)$, set

   556		$\{1,\dots,m\}$; for $m+1 \le j \le 2m$, $i_X$ is uniformly random and
   557		$i_Z = j - m$; for $2m+1 \le j \le 2m+2$, both $i_X$ and $i_Z$ are
   558		uniformly random; and $v'_X, v'_Z$ are the canonical line

   562		direction $w = (w_X, w_Z, \gamma, \delta)$ whose first nonzero
